title: Urban mining: Africa’s hidden mineral economy
body:
As Africa debates mineral beneficiation, one opportunity remains largely overlooked: urban mining.

Across cities like Abidjan, Accra, Lagos, and Dar es Salaam, a sophisticated—yet largely invisible—system already exists for recovering valuable materials from discarded electronics. Informal e-waste networks collect, dismantle, repair, and recover metals from phones, computers, cables, and household appliances every single day.

These workers extract copper, aluminum, and precious metals—materials that are fundamental to modern industrial systems, such as renewable energy, electrical infrastructure, and electronics manufacturing.

And Yes. These are the same metals Africa exports from its mines. They are the same materials around which African governments are now designing “beyond extraction” industrial policies aimed at capturing more value domestically.

Yet there is a striking contradiction. Most recovered materials still leave the continent as low-value scrap, exported abroad for refining and reprocessing. Meanwhile, the informal workers who recover these materials often remain trapped in precarious livelihoods.

This is more than a waste-management issue. It is a major industrial policy blind spot.

Urban mining could become a new pillar of Africa’s mineral industrialization strategy, linking circular economy systems, informal employment, and strategic mineral value chains.

As global demand for recycled materials rises—and as industries seek lower-carbon inputs—the strategic value of recovered metals will only grow.

So what needs to change?

- Build small-scale refining capacity. Cities that generate large volumes of e-waste should host modular recycling and refining facilities capable of upgrading scrap into industrial-grade metals.
- Integrate informal collectors into formal value chains. Policy should focus on formalization, training, and safer working conditions rather than displacement.
- Develop certification systems for recycled minerals. Traceable “recycled African metals” could become attractive inputs for global manufacturers seeking low-carbon and responsibly sourced materials.
- Link urban mining to broader industrial policy. Recovered metals can feed domestic industries such as electronics repair, electrical manufacturing, renewable energy systems, and battery assembly.

The reality is this: Africa’s mineral strategies are often framed around what lies beneath the ground. However, a growing share of strategic materials already exists above ground—in cities, landfills, repair markets, and scrap networks.

Recognizing and investing in this reality could transform Africa’s expanding urban waste streams into a new frontier for mineral-based industrialization.

**Bottom line:** The future of Africa’s mineral economy may not only be in its mines. It may also be in its cities.
